hook: The organiser of the Persian Empire, whose royal couriers inspired the US Postal Service's motto.

pages.x: In 522 BC Darius and six other nobles killed the king, who they claimed was an impostor. Herodotus says the seven agreed that the man whose horse neighed first at sunrise would be king. Darius's groom made sure his horse had a reason to neigh.

Darius had his victories over nine rebel kings carved high on a cliff face, in three languages. In the 1830s a British officer, Henry Rawlinson, copied it while dangling on ropes. It became the key to reading cuneiform, the world's oldest writing, as the Rosetta Stone was for hieroglyphs.

Darius split his empire into about twenty provinces, each with a governor, a tax and a royal spy. He built the Royal Road, 2,700 km from Susa to Sardis, with fresh horses every day's ride, and minted gold coins. Herodotus wrote that nothing stopped his couriers, "neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night".

He began a great palace city at Persepolis for the New Year festival. On the stairs of its hall, carved men from 23 nations, Egyptians, Indians, Ethiopians, Greeks and others, bring tribute to the king. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BC, but its columns still stand.

In 490 BC he sent an army to punish Athens for helping Greek cities in Asia rebel. It was beaten at Marathon, near Athens. Darius died in 486 BC while planning a bigger invasion, which his son Xerxes would lead.

Darius turned the conquests of Cyrus into a working state, with provinces, taxes, laws, coins and roads that later empires copied. At its height his empire stretched from Egypt and Greece to India and ruled a larger share of the world's people than any empire before or since.
pts: Organised the Persian Empire into provinces
Built the Royal Road and its courier service
Left the inscription that unlocked cuneiform
